assessment.nobel_worthiness: A highly influential empirical account of how trade and technological change reshape local labour demand, occupations and wage inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson provide a coherent and identifiable core for the task-and-trade-shock research programme.
assessment.maturity: The evidence and its influence on labour economics and public debate have accumulated over a long period.
uncertainties: The relative contribution of trade shocks versus broader technological change remains contested.
The wider literature has contributors beyond the proposed trio.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work made adverse selection in insurance empirically measurable and linked rigorous evidence to central economic theory and policy design.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein, Einav and Salanie represent complementary theoretical and empirical contributions to the stated discovery.
assessment.maturity: The research programme is mature, replicated across settings and consequential for health and insurance economics.
uncertainties: The appropriate boundary between adverse selection, moral hazard and market-design contributions is not fully sharp.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification established a principled way to make credible claims when data cannot justify point identification.
assessment.attribution: Manski is foundational, while Tamer and Molinari are central to the development of moment-inequality and inference methods.
assessment.maturity: The ideas are long established and broadly used in applied and theoretical econometrics.
uncertainties: Its practical influence is substantial but less visibly unified than that of some empirical discoveries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Audit and correspondence methods produced persuasive evidence on discrimination and changed empirical labour-market research.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are especially central to the modern audit-study landmark; Charles supplies major related labour-market research.
assessment.maturity: The approach has been repeatedly deployed internationally and remains highly policy relevant.
uncertainties: Audit outcomes identify treatment at particular margins and do not by themselves measure all mechanisms or aggregate discrimination.
Credit within the broader audit-study tradition is difficult to delimit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic-panel GMM methods transformed empirical work with longitudinal microeconomic data and enabled credible treatment of persistent outcomes and endogeneity.
assessment.attribution: Arellano, Blundell and Bond have clear, complementary claims to the core estimators and their development.
assessment.maturity: The methods have been standard tools for decades across economics.
uncertainties: Routine widespread use does not always imply reliable application, given sensitivity to instruments and specification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population administrative data yielded a new empirical map of intergenerational mobility and made neighbourhood and policy differences salient.
assessment.attribution: Chetty and Hendren are central to the modern mobility evidence, with Katz an important collaborator in the programme.
assessment.maturity: The work has generated extensive subsequent research and has clear public-policy significance.
uncertainties: The literature is comparatively recent relative to other leading candidates.
Measurement advances and causal interpretation should be distinguished carefully.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantile regression made distributional heterogeneity tractable and has had enduring effects throughout empirical economics.
assessment.attribution: Koenker and Bassett originated the central method; Chernozhukov made influential later contributions to distributional econometrics.
assessment.maturity: The framework is mature, widely taught and used across many fields.
uncertainties: The broad modern distributional-methods label may make the contribution less sharply bounded than the original quantile-regression innovation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This research established that early-life health and environments have durable economic consequences and focused attention on dynamic skill formation.
assessment.attribution: Currie and Almond are central to credible empirical evidence on early-life conditions, while Cunha is central to the dynamic human-capital framework.
assessment.maturity: The programme is mature and influential in health, education and labour economics.
uncertainties: The empirical and theoretical strands have partly distinct origins.
The broad early-life literature has many important contributors.
